title: Given an array of numbers, find the maximum sum of any strictly increasing subsequence. Explain how the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program adapts to maximise sum instead of length, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence (Rising Subsequence with the Largest Total)
keyPoints: Each index holds the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at that element, seeded with the element's own value.
For each index i, look back at every earlier index j with a strictly smaller value and take the best extension.
The answer is the maximum sum across all indices because the best subsequence can end anywhere.
This mirrors the LIS structure but swaps counting elements for summing values.
The value objective prevents the tails-array O(n log n) speedup that works for the length version, keeping this O(n^2).
In banking, this finds the rising deposit subsequence whose amounts sum to the most.

s1_definition.oneliner: Find the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence by seeding each index with its own value and extending from the best earlier smaller-value sum.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sum objective** – instead of counting elements (LIS), sum their values to find the heaviest rising subsequence.
- **Seed** – each dp[i] starts as the element's own value, because a single element is a valid rising subsequence.
- **Extension** – for each i, look back at every j < i where a[j] < a[i] and set dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + a[i]).
- **Global answer** – the answer is the maximum dp[i] across all indices, because the best subsequence can end anywhere.
- **O(n^2) time** – the nested loop checks every earlier index for each position.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks at a customer's series of deposit amounts and finds the strictly rising subsequence of deposits whose total amount is the largest. The bank rewards customers whose deposits show growing discipline, and the prize goes to the sequence with the biggest sum.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence adapts the Longest Increasing Subsequence DP by swapping the objective from counting elements to summing values. For each index you compute the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at that element, seeded with the element's own value because a single element is a valid subsequence on its own.

To extend, you look back at every earlier index holding a strictly smaller value. The increasing subsequence ending there can be continued by the current element, so the new sum is dp[j] + a[i]. You take the maximum over all such extensions. The global answer is the maximum dp[i] across all indices because the best subsequence can end anywhere.

At the National Bank of India, the rewards team examined a customer's deposit history and found the strictly rising subsequence with the largest total, rewarding customers whose deposits showed strong growing discipline. The nested-loop DP computed the answer in O(n^2) time.

The senior-level insight is that the value objective prevents the O(n log n) tails-array speedup that works for LIS. The tails trick relies on a monotonic relationship between subsequence length and the smallest ending value, which breaks when the objective is sum instead of count. This is why MSIS stays at O(n^2).

Remember one sentence: seed each index with its own value, extend from the best earlier smaller sum, and the global maximum is the answer.
